claim: Cells lacking PTEN strongly overproliferated specifically in nutrient restricted larvae.
source: Cells lacking PTEN strongly overproliferated specifically in nutrient restricted larvae.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations shown in multiple figures (Figure 2B-E) demonstrating increased clone size under nutrient restriction conditions.

claim: PTEN mutant cells were sensitive to starvation.
source: Although the PTEN mutant cells were sensitive to starvation, they successfully competed with neighboring cells by autonomous and non-autonomous mechanisms distinct from cell competition.
evidence: Supported by data showing that hypomorphic PTEN larvae did not survive to pupariation when reared on 10 g/l yeast food (Figure 1C).

claim: PTEN mutant cells successfully competed with neighboring cells by autonomous and non-autonomous mechanisms distinct from cell competition.
source: Although the PTEN mutant cells were sensitive to starvation, they successfully competed with neighboring cells by autonomous and non-autonomous mechanisms distinct from cell competition.
evidence: Supported by data showing reduction of surrounding tissue (Figure 2B), non-autonomous effects on P-PKB levels (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), and systemic effects on body size (Figure 6B-D).

claim: The overgrowth of PTEN mutant cells was strictly dependent on the activity of Akt/PKB.
source: The overgrowth was strictly dependent on the activity of the downstream components Akt/PKB and TORC1
evidence: Demonstrated by complete suppression of PTEN overgrowth when PKB function was reduced or removed (Figure 4C).

claim: The overgrowth of PTEN mutant cells was strictly dependent on TORC1 activity.
source: The overgrowth was strictly dependent on the activity of the downstream components Akt/PKB and TORC1
evidence: Supported by suppression of overgrowth when TORC1 activity was inhibited by overexpression of Tsc1/2 (Figure 4F-G) or by removing Rheb function (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).

claim: A reduction in amino acid uptake by reducing the levels of the amino acid transporter Slimfast caused clones of PTEN mutant cells to collapse.
source: a reduction in amino acid uptake by reducing the levels of the amino acid transporter Slimfast caused clones of PTEN mutant cells to collapse.
evidence: Demonstrated by massive increase in apoptosis and elimination of PTEN mutant tissue when Slimfast was knocked down under starvation conditions (Figure 5A-B).

claim: PTEN is the second most frequently mutated tumor suppressor found in many types of human cancers.
source: PTEN is well conserved from flies to humans, and it is the second most frequently mutated tumor suppressor found in many types of human cancers (Goberdhan and Wilson, 2003; Salmena et al., 2008; Hollander et al., 2011; Song et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: PTEN antagonizes the function of the lipid kinase Phosphatidylinositide 3-kinase (PI3K).
source: PTEN antagonizes the function of the lipid kinase Phosphatidylinositide 3-kinase (PI3K); therefore, in the absence of PTEN, high levels of the lipid second messenger PIP3 result in an increased membrane recruitment and activation of the serine/threonine kinase PKB (protein kinase B, also known as Akt), which leads to enhanced cellular growth, proliferation, and survival (Altomare and Testa, 2005; Georgescu, 2010; Song et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citations.

claim: In the absence of PTEN, high levels of PIP3 result in increased membrane recruitment and activation of PKB.
source: PTEN antagonizes the function of the lipid kinase Phosphatidylinositide 3-kinase (PI3K); therefore, in the absence of PTEN, high levels of the lipid second messenger PIP3 result in an increased membrane recruitment and activation of the serine/threonine kinase PKB (protein kinase B, also known as Akt), which leads to enhanced cellular growth, proliferation, and survival (Altomare and Testa, 2005; Georgescu, 2010; Song et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by both citations and experimental data showing elevated PIP3 and P-PKB levels in PTEN mutant tissue (Figure 4A-B).

claim: Activation of PKB leads to enhanced cellular growth, proliferation, and survival.
source: PTEN antagonizes the function of the lipid kinase Phosphatidylinositide 3-kinase (PI3K); therefore, in the absence of PTEN, high levels of the lipid second messenger PIP3 result in an increased membrane recruitment and activation of the serine/threonine kinase PKB (protein kinase B, also known as Akt), which leads to enhanced cellular growth, proliferation, and survival (Altomare and Testa, 2005; Georgescu, 2010; Song et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Cells overexpressing Dp110/PI3K are enlarged and increase their nutrient storage in the fat body.
source: Cells overexpressing Dp110/PI3K are enlarged and, in the fat body, increase their nutrient storage.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Britton et al., 2002.

claim: Nutrient stockpiling in PI3K overexpressing cells helps them to cell-autonomously bypass nutritional requirements for cellular growth and DNA replication during amino acid deprivation.
source: This stockpiling of nutrients helps them to cell-autonomously bypass the nutritional requirements for cellular growth and DNA replication during amino acid deprivation (Britton et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Britton et al., 2002.

claim: In mitotic tissues, clones of PTEN mutant cells are enlarged, which is mainly caused by an increase in cell size.
source: In mitotic tissues, clones of PTEN mutant cells are enlarged, which is mainly caused by an increase in cell size (Leevers et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Leevers et al., 1996.

claim: The overgrowth caused by the loss of PTEN is rather mild.
source: However, given the importance of PTEN as a tumor suppressor, the overgrowth caused by the loss of PTEN is rather mild (Goberdhan et al., 1999; Huang et al., 1999; Gao et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Tumors lacking PTEN or with increased PI3K activity are resistant to dietary restriction.
source: Recently, it has been demonstrated that tumors lacking PTEN or with increased PI3K activity are resistant to dietary restriction (Kalaany and Sabatini, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kalaany and Sabatini, 2009.

claim: Down to 50 g/l yeast, larvae can be regarded as fully fed since the developmental time, weight, and survival were not affected.
source: Down to 50 g/l yeast, larvae can be regarded as fully fed since the developmental time, weight, and survival were not affected.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A-B.

claim: At a yeast concentration range between 50 g/l and 10 g/l, the development was gradually delayed and the weight decreased.
source: At a yeast concentration range between 50 g/l and 10 g/l, the development was gradually delayed and the weight decreased.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A-B.

claim: The yeast concentration range between 50 g/l and 10 g/l can be regarded as mild starvation, since survival was not compromised down to 25 g/l yeast concentration.
source: This phase can be regarded as mild starvation, since survival was not compromised down to 25 g/l yeast concentration.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Reduction of the yeast concentration to and below 10 g/l increased the developmental time from first instar to pupa and severely decreased body weight.
source: Reduction of the yeast concentration to and below 10 g/l increased the developmental time from first instar to pupa and severely decreased body weight.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A-B.

claim: Yeast concentration at and below 10 g/l is regarded as severe starvation because mortality was increased.
source: Since mortality was also increased, this phase is regarded as severe starvation.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The turning point between mild starvation and severe starvation is approximately at 10 g/l concentration of yeast.
source: Based on these results, the turning point between mild starvation and severe starvation is approximately at 10 g/l concentration of yeast.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data shown in Figure 1A-B.

claim: Fully fed hypomorphic PKB mutants weighed approximately the same as wild-type flies reared on 10 g/l yeast food.
source: Interestingly, fully fed hypomorphic PKB mutants weighed approximately the same as wild-type flies reared on 10 g/l yeast food.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: When reared on 10 g/l yeast food, PKB mutants were further delayed but only mildly decreased in size and weight.
source: When reared on 10 g/l yeast food, PKB mutants were further delayed but only mildly decreased in size and weight (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C-D.

claim: Hypomorphic PTEN larvae and adult flies were larger than wild-type controls under normal food conditions.
source: In contrast, hypomorphic PTEN larvae and adult flies were larger than wild-type controls under normal food conditions (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The eye and wing imaginal discs of hypomorphic PTEN larvae were larger compared to control discs under both normal and starvation conditions.
source: The prospective adult tissues, the eye and wing imaginal discs, were larger compared to control discs under both conditions (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: PTEN hypomorphic larvae were highly sensitive to a reduction in yeast content and did not survive to pupariation when reared on 10 g/l yeast food.
source: PTEN hypomorphic larvae were highly sensitive to a reduction in yeast content, and although still larger, they did not survive to pupariation when reared on 10 g/l yeast food (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Larvae with randomly induced PI3K overexpression clones are starvation sensitive.
source: This is consistent with the findings that larvae with randomly induced PI3K overexpression clones are starvation sensitive (Britton et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Britton et al., 2002.

claim: Under nutrient restriction conditions, insulin signaling needs to be dampened to allow for survival of the organism.
source: Thus, under NR conditions, insulin signaling needs to be dampened to allow for survival of the organism.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that PKB mutants survive better under starvation while PTEN mutants do not.

claim: Tumors with elevated PI3K activity are starvation resistant.
source: In contrast to the situation at the organismal level, tumors with elevated PI3K activity are starvation resistant (Kalaany and Sabatini, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kalaany and Sabatini, 2009.

claim: Under mild starvation conditions (30 g/l yeast), PTEN clones were further increased in size, resulting in an overall increase in disc size as compared to discs harboring control clones.
source: Under mild starvation conditions (30 g/l yeast), PTEN clones were further increased in size, resulting in an overall increase in disc size as compared to discs harboring control clones.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Reducing the yeast concentration to 20 g/l and below led to a massive size increase of the PTEN clones and to a concomitant reduction of the surrounding tissue.
source: Reducing the yeast concentration to 20 g/l and below led to a massive size increase of the PTEN clones and to a concomitant reduction of the surrounding tissue.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: PTEN clones had fused and rendered the discs lobed in appearance at 20 g/l yeast and below.
source: Furthermore, the PTEN clones had fused and rendered the discs lobed in appearance (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: At 5 g/l yeast concentration, the eye discs with PTEN mutant tissue were severely overgrown with polyp-like structures protruding from the discs.
source: At 5 g/l yeast concentration, the eye discs with PTEN mutant tissue were severely overgrown with polyp-like structures protruding from the discs (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Adult eyes with PTEN clones reared on 5 g/l yeast displayed strong malformations and outgrowths, indicating a loss of epithelial integrity.
source: The resulting adult eyes displayed strong malformations and outgrowths, indicating a loss of epithelial integrity (Figure 2—figure supplement 1, red squares).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: In some cases, no PTEN clones could be recovered in the adult eyes, probably due to a collapse of the PTEN clones resulting in melanized scars.
source: In some cases, no clones could be recovered in the adult eyes, probably due to a collapse of the PTEN clones resulting in melanized scars (Figure 2—figure supplement 3, white arrow).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Tangential eye sections did not reveal any structural defects in ommatidial arrangement in PTEN mutant eyes.
source: Tangential eye sections did not reveal any structural defects in ommatidial arrangement (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: PTEN mutant cells overgrow in a cell-autonomous manner as the enlarged ommatidia were exclusively composed of mutant cells.
source: PTEN mutant cells overgrow in a cell-autonomous manner as the enlarged ommatidia were exclusively composed of mutant cells.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: The overgrowth phenotype of PTEN clones is not specific to the eye; it was also observed in other imaginal tissues like the wing disc.
source: The overgrowth phenotype of PTEN clones is not specific to the eye; it was also observed in other imaginal tissues like the wing disc (Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5.

claim: Already 36 hr after clone induction, the PTEN clones were increased in size.
source: Already 36 hr after clone induction, the PTEN clones were increased in size, and the overgrowth of PTEN clones and the reduction in wild-type tissue were fully apparent after 60 hr (Figure 2C)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The overgrowth of PTEN clones and the reduction in wild-type tissue were fully apparent after 60 hr.
source: Already 36 hr after clone induction, the PTEN clones were increased in size, and the overgrowth of PTEN clones and the reduction in wild-type tissue were fully apparent after 60 hr (Figure 2C)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The developmental delay is not the main cause of the overgrowth of PTEN clones.
source: Already 36 hr after clone induction, the PTEN clones were increased in size, and the overgrowth of PTEN clones and the reduction in wild-type tissue were fully apparent after 60 hr (Figure 2C), excluding the developmental delay as a main cause of the overgrowth.
evidence: This is an inference based on the time-course data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: When the transfer from starvation to normal food occurred within the first 72 hr, the overgrowth of the PTEN clones was efficiently rescued.
source: When the transfer from starvation to normal food occurred within the first 72 hr, the overgrowth of the PTEN clones was efficiently rescued.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 6.

claim: It was sufficient to transfer larvae within the first 48 hr from normal to starvation food to produce the overgrowth phenotype.
source: Consistently, it was sufficient to transfer larvae within the first 48 hr from normal to starvation food to produce the overgrowth phenotype.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 6.

claim: The initial stages after clone induction are important for PTEN clones to develop the overgrowth phenotype.
source: After this time point, PTEN clones did not acquire the full growth advantage over the surrounding tissue, confirming the importance of the initial stages for PTEN clones to develop the overgrowth phenotype (Figure 2—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is an inference based on the food switch experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 6.

claim: Under starvation conditions, the mutant tissue occupied most of the adult eye and the wild-type tissue was severely reduced.
source: Under starvation conditions, the mutant tissue occupied most of the adult eye and the wild-type tissue was severely reduced.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The overrepresentation of PTEN mutant tissue resulted in an absolute increase of eye size under starvation as compared to normal food conditions.
source: This overrepresentation of the mutant tissue resulted in an absolute increase of eye size under starvation as compared to normal food conditions (Figure 2D,D′).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D,D′.

claim: Under normal food conditions, the eye size increase in PTEN mutant eyes was mainly caused by larger ommatidia (+27%), and to a minor extent by more ommatidia (+14%).
source: Under normal food conditions, the eye size increase was mainly caused by larger ommatidia (+27%), and to a minor extent by more ommatidia (+14%).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E-E′′.

claim: Under 10 g/l yeast food, the ommatidial size was roughly proportionally reduced in wild-type and PTEN mutant eyes.
source: Under 10 g/l yeast food, the ommatidial size was roughly proportionally reduced in wild-type and PTEN mutant eyes.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E-E′′.

claim: Under 10 g/l yeast food, the ommatidia number was decreased by 6% in wild-type eyes but was massively increased in PTEN mutant eyes (+44%).
source: Intriguingly, whereas the ommatidia number was decreased by 6% in wild-type eyes, it was massively increased in PTEN mutant eyes (+44%).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E-E′′.

claim: The PTEN mutant tissue displays a switch from hypertrophy to hyperplasia under starvation.
source: Thus, the PTEN mutant tissue displays a switch from hypertrophy to hyperplasia.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data showing increased cell number rather than cell size under starvation (Figure 2E-E′′).

claim: Only few apoptotic cells were detected in the heterozygous tissue under both fed and starving conditions.
source: Whereas only few apoptotic cells were detected in the heterozygous tissue under both fed and starving conditions, increased levels of apoptosis were observed within the overgrowing PTEN clones (Figure 3A,A′).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A,A′.

claim: Increased levels of apoptosis were observed within the overgrowing PTEN clones.
source: Whereas only few apoptotic cells were detected in the heterozygous tissue under both fed and starving conditions, increased levels of apoptosis were observed within the overgrowing PTEN clones (Figure 3A,A′).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A,A′.

claim: Most of the apoptosis in 48 hr PTEN clones was observed in the mutant tissue, arguing against a major role of cell competition in the overgrowth phenotype.
source: Again, most of the apoptosis was observed in the mutant tissue, arguing against a major role of cell competition in the overgrowth phenotype.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Expression of p35 exclusively in the PTEN clones efficiently blocked apoptosis and enhanced the overgrowth.
source: Expression of p35 or of dominant negative JNK (bskDN; Adachi-Yamada et al., 1999) exclusively in the PTEN clones (by means of the MARCM system) efficiently blocked apoptosis and enhanced the overgrowth (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, and not shown).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: PTEN clones overgrew even more in the dorsal compartment when p35 was expressed there, and the surrounding tissue still got strongly reduced.
source: Consistent with the above results and the apoptosis pattern, PTEN clones overgrew even more in the dorsal compartment, and the surrounding tissue still got strongly reduced.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The cells neighboring PTEN clones are not eliminated by apoptosis.
source: Thus, the cells neighboring PTEN clones are not eliminated by apoptosis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the p35 expression experiment shown in Figure 3D.

claim: PTEN clones were overgrown irrespective of blocking JNK signaling in neighboring cells.
source: However, PTEN clones were overgrown irrespective of blocking JNK signaling in neighboring cells (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Under severe starvation (5 g/l yeast content), the PTEN mutant polyp-like structures outgrowing from the eye discs exhibited very high levels of apoptosis.
source: Under severe starvation (5 g/l yeast content), the PTEN mutant polyp-like structures outgrowing from the eye discs exhibited very high levels of apoptosis (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Eyes with collapsed PTEN clones contained more wild-type cells, indicating that the lost PTEN mutant tissue was compensated for.
source: Those eyes contained more wild-type cells, indicating that the lost PTEN mutant tissue was compensated for.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: PTEN mutant cells are running at the edge of survival under limited nutrient conditions.
source: Thus, PTEN mutant cells are running at the edge of survival under limited nutrient conditions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the high apoptosis levels and collapse of clones under severe starvation.

claim: PTEN mutant cells start to disobey the organ boundaries but are prone to apoptosis.
source: They start to disobey the organ boundaries but are prone to apoptosis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the polyp-like structures and high apoptosis levels.

claim: The GFP–PH domain fusion protein was strongly localized at the membrane under both fed and NR conditions in PTEN clones.
source: The GFP–PH domain fusion protein was strongly localized at the membrane under both fed and NR conditions in PTEN clones.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The tGPH reporter signal was diffuse in the cytoplasm in the surrounding tissue under both fed and NR conditions.
source: In contrast, the reporter signal was diffuse in the cytoplasm in the surrounding tissue under both conditions.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Removal of Insulin receptor (InR) function from the PTEN mutant tissue only slightly reduced the overgrowth.
source: Removal of Insulin receptor (InR) function from the PTEN mutant tissue only slightly reduced the overgrowth.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: In the absence of PTEN, the cellular PIP3 levels are sufficient to sustain the overgrowth regardless of the upstream signaling.
source: Thus, in the absence of PTEN, the cellular PIP3 levels are sufficient to sustain the overgrowth regardless of the upstream signaling (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an inference based on the InR removal experiment shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Elevated levels of phosphorylated PKB (P-PKB) were found at the membrane in PTEN clones at 100 g/l and 10 g/l yeast content.
source: Similarly, elevated levels of phosphorylated PKB (P-PKB) were found at the membrane in PTEN clones at 100 g/l and 10 g/l yeast content (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The total levels of PKB were decreased in PTEN mutant tissue under both conditions as compared to the control under normal food conditions.
source: Although the total levels of PKB were decreased in PTEN mutant tissue under both conditions as compared to the control under normal food conditions, the P-PKB levels were elevated.
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The P-PKB levels were elevated in PTEN mutant tissue under both fed and starvation conditions.
source: Although the total levels of PKB were decreased in PTEN mutant tissue under both conditions as compared to the control under normal food conditions, the P-PKB levels were elevated.
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: High PIP3 levels result in robust PKB activation under standard and starvation conditions.
source: Thus, high PIP3 levels result in robust PKB activation under standard and starvation conditions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the P-PKB data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Reducing or removing PKB function completely suppressed the PTEN overgrowth under normal as well as under starvation conditions.
source: Consistently, reducing or removing PKB function by using a PH-domain mutant (Stocker et al., 2002) and a kinase-dead PKB (Staveley et al., 1998), respectively, completely suppressed the PTEN overgrowth under normal as well as under starvation conditions (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: FoxO is phosphorylated by PKB and sequestered in the cytoplasm upon high PI3K signaling activity.
source: Upon high PI3K signaling activity, FoxO is phosphorylated by PKB and sequestered in the cytoplasm, and FoxO-mediated transcription of growth-suppressing genes is thus inhibited (Brunet et al., 1999; Kops et al., 1999; Burgering and Kops, 2002).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citations.

claim: FoxO was localized in the cytoplasm in PTEN mutant tissue under both fed and starvation conditions.
source: FoxO was localized in the cytoplasm in PTEN mutant tissue under both conditions, whereas starvation induced the shuttling of FoxO into nuclei in the control tissue (Figure 4E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Starvation induced the shuttling of FoxO into nuclei in the control tissue.
source: FoxO was localized in the cytoplasm in PTEN mutant tissue under both conditions, whereas starvation induced the shuttling of FoxO into nuclei in the control tissue (Figure 4E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Overexpression of FoxO decreases eye size, which is exacerbated under starvation conditions.
source: It has been shown that overexpression of FoxO decreases eye size, which is exacerbated under starvation conditions (Junger et al., 2003; Kramer et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The FoxO-induced eye size reduction was not observed in PTEN clones.
source: Consistent with the inactivation of FoxO in PTEN mutant cells, the FoxO-induced eye size reduction was not observed in PTEN clones (Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplements 3 and 4).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplements 3 and 4.

claim: PTEN mutant cells did respond to starvation by reducing the levels of S6K and of phosphorylated S6K (P-S6K).
source: PTEN mutant cells did respond to starvation by reducing the levels of S6K and of phosphorylated S6K (P-S6K), as revealed by Western blot analysis on discs bearing eyFlp/FRT cell lethal clones of PTEN (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: PKB signaling activity was slightly reduced in PTEN mutant cells under starvation as compared to standard conditions.
source: PKB signaling activity was also slightly reduced as compared to standard conditions (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Reducing TORC1 activity suppressed the overgrowth of the PTEN mutant tissue.
source: Reducing TORC1 activity suppressed the overgrowth of the PTEN mutant tissue (Figure 4F,G, 4G′ and Figure 4—figure supplement 5).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F,G, 4G′ and Figure 4—figure supplement 5.

claim: P-PKB levels were increased in PTEN mutant tissue with reduced TORC1 activity under both fed and NR conditions.
source: P-PKB levels, however, were increased in the mutant tissue under both fed and NR conditions (Figure 4—figure supplement 6), which is in agreement with the negative feedback regulation of TORC1 on the activation of PKB (Radimerski et al., 2002; Kockel et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 6.

claim: TORC1 negatively regulates the activation of PKB through feedback regulation.
source: P-PKB levels, however, were increased in the mutant tissue under both fed and NR conditions (Figure 4—figure supplement 6), which is in agreement with the negative feedback regulation of TORC1 on the activation of PKB (Radimerski et al., 2002; Kockel et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The overgrowth of PTEN clones strictly depends on normal TORC1 function.
source: Eyes mutant for PTEN and a hypomorphic allele of TOR were reduced to the size of control eyes at both fed and starved conditions, indicating that the overgrowth of PTEN clones strictly depends on normal TORC1 function (Figure 4—figure supplement 7).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 7.

claim: The size reduction of PTEN clones caused by impaired TORC1 function was primarily due to smaller ommatidia under normal conditions.
source: Interestingly, whereas the size reduction of PTEN clones caused by impaired TORC1 function was primarily due to smaller ommatidia under normal conditions, ommatidia size was only slightly affected under starvation.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 7.

claim: The hyperproliferation observed in PTEN clones under NR was almost completely abolished by impaired TORC1 function.
source: By contrast, the hyperproliferation observed in PTEN clones under NR was almost completely abolished (Figure 4—figure supplement 7).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 7.

claim: TORC1 is indispensable for the switch to hyperproliferation observed in PTEN mutant tissue upon NR.
source: Thus, TORC1 is indispensable for the switch to hyperproliferation observed in PTEN mutant tissue upon NR.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data showing that TORC1 inhibition abolishes hyperproliferation under starvation.

claim: Slimfast (Slif) has been shown to activate TOR signaling in the fat body.
source: The cationic amino acid transporter Slimfast (Slif) has been shown to activate TOR signaling in the fat body, and it appears to be an important component of a systemic nutrient sensor mechanism (Colombani et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Colombani et al., 2003.

claim: Slif appears to be an important component of a systemic nutrient sensor mechanism.
source: The cationic amino acid transporter Slimfast (Slif) has been shown to activate TOR signaling in the fat body, and it appears to be an important component of a systemic nutrient sensor mechanism (Colombani et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Colombani et al., 2003.

claim: Slif function is required in mitotic tissues, as clones in which Slif has been knocked down are reduced in size.
source: Slif function is also required in mitotic tissues, as clones in which Slif has been knocked down (Slifanti) are reduced in size, possibly due to reduced TORC1 activation.
evidence: This is established knowledge based on previous studies.

claim: Expressing Slifanti in PTEN clones resulted in a slight reduction of the mutant tissue under normal conditions.
source: Whereas expressing Slifanti in PTEN clones resulted in a slight reduction of the mutant tissue under normal conditions, it caused a nearly complete elimination of the PTEN mutant tissue under starvation conditions, while not affecting the control clones (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Expressing Slifanti in PTEN clones caused a nearly complete elimination of the PTEN mutant tissue under starvation conditions.
source: Whereas expressing Slifanti in PTEN clones resulted in a slight reduction of the mutant tissue under normal conditions, it caused a nearly complete elimination of the PTEN mutant tissue under starvation conditions, while not affecting the control clones (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The loss of PTEN mutant tissue with Slif knockdown was accompanied by a massive increase in apoptosis.
source: The loss of PTEN mutant tissue was accompanied by a massive increase in apoptosis, and GFP-positive (and thus PTEN mutant) cellular remnants were scattered throughout the disc (Figure 5B)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: PTEN clones collapsed after an initial overgrowth when Slif was knocked down.
source: The loss of PTEN mutant tissue was accompanied by a massive increase in apoptosis, and GFP-positive (and thus PTEN mutant) cellular remnants were scattered throughout the disc (Figure 5B), suggesting that PTEN clones collapsed after an initial overgrowth.
evidence: This is an inference based on the apoptosis data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Early overgrowth of PTEN clones and high P-PKB signals were observed under starvation when Slif was knocked down.
source: Indeed, early overgrowth of PTEN clones and high P-PKB signals were observed under starvation (Figure 5C upper panel).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C upper panel.

claim: Slif function became limiting in PTEN clones that were subsequently eliminated.
source: Later, Slif function became limiting in PTEN clones that were subsequently eliminated (Figure 5A,C lower panel).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A,C lower panel.

claim: The structure of adult eyes that had lost the PTEN clones with Slif knockdown was completely normal.
source: Intriguingly, the structure of the resulting adult eyes that had lost the PTEN clones was completely normal, indicating that the surrounding tissue was able to compensate for the loss of the clones (Figure 5D,D′).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D,D′.

claim: The surrounding tissue was able to compensate for the loss of PTEN clones with Slif knockdown.
source: Intriguingly, the structure of the resulting adult eyes that had lost the PTEN clones was completely normal, indicating that the surrounding tissue was able to compensate for the loss of the clones (Figure 5D,D′).
evidence: This is an inference based on the normal eye structure shown in Figure 5D,D′.

claim: The effects that the reduction of Slimfast exerted on PTEN clones are distinct from those resulting from inhibiting TORC1 function.
source: The effects that the reduction of Slimfast exerted on PTEN clones are distinct from those resulting from inhibiting TORC1 function, as overexpression of Tsc1/2 suppressed the overgrowth of PTEN clones already at an early stage (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is an inference based on comparing the effects of Slif knockdown and Tsc1/2 overexpression.

claim: Rather than the activation of TORC1, another aspect of Slif function—probably the amino acid influx itself—is critical for the survival of the PTEN mutant tissue.
source: This may indicate that, rather than the activation of TORC1, another aspect of Slif function—probably the amino acid influx itself—is critical for the survival of the PTEN mutant tissue.
evidence: This is speculation based on the distinct effects of Slif knockdown versus TORC1 inhibition.

claim: Reducing Atg5 did not impact on the initial growth of PTEN clones with reduced Slif function.
source: However, reducing Atg5, a key component of the autophagic machinery, did not impact on the initial growth of PTEN clones with reduced Slif function (Figure 5—figure supplements 1 and 3).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplements 1 and 3.

claim: Blocking apoptosis (by means of p35 expression) in PTEN clones with diminished Slif function delays the collapse of the clones.
source: Blocking apoptosis (by means of p35 expression) in PTEN clones with diminished Slif function delays the collapse of the clones as the clones can still be detected in imaginal discs (Figure 5—figure supplements 1 and 2) but are absent from adult eyes (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplements 1, 2, and 3.

claim: P-PKB levels in the wild-type tissue neighboring with PTEN clones were reduced as compared to the tissue neighboring with control clones.
source: P-PKB levels in the wild-type tissue neighboring with PTEN clones were reduced as compared to the tissue neighboring with control clones (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Knocking down PTEN in the dorsal part of the eye resulted in its size increase and reduced the size of the ventral part as compared to control eyes.
source: Knocking down PTEN in the dorsal part of the eye not only resulted in its size increase, but also reduced the size of the ventral part as compared to control eyes (Figure 6A,A′).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A,A′.

claim: The growth-reducing effect of PTEN knockdown within the eye was already visible under standard conditions but further enhanced on 10 g/l yeast food.
source: This growth-reducing effect within the eye was already visible under standard conditions but further enhanced on 10 g/l yeast food.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A,A′.

claim: RNAi-mediated knockdown of PTEN did not result in enhanced overgrowth under starvation as compared to standard conditions.
source: In contrast to the null mutant situation, RNAi-mediated knockdown of PTEN did not result in enhanced overgrowth under starvation as compared to standard conditions, probably due to residual PTEN in the knockdown situation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of RNAi knockdown versus null mutant phenotypes.

claim: Flies with PTEN mutant heads have smaller bodies as judged by shoulder area under starvation conditions.
source: Flies with PTEN mutant heads have smaller bodies as judged by shoulder area (s.a.) under starvation conditions.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Wings of flies with PTEN mutant heads under starvation are smaller than wings of control flies.
source: Wings of flies with PTEN mutant heads under starvation are smaller than wings of control flies.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C,C′.

claim: Size of fat body nuclei of larvae with PTEN mutant eye discs is decreased under starvation as compared to the control.
source: Size of fat body nuclei of larvae with PTEN mutant eye discs is decreased under starvation as compared to the control.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D,D′.

claim: The growth-reducing non-autonomous effect of PTEN mutant tissue acts systemically.
source: Thus, the growth-reducing non-autonomous effect of PTEN mutant tissue acts systemically.
evidence: This is an inference based on the systemic effects on body size, wing size, and fat body shown in Figure 6B-D.

claim: The PTEN mutant tissue efficiently competes with other larval tissues for common resources to support their massive growth.
source: The observed non-autonomous effects suggest that the PTEN mutant tissue efficiently competes with other larval tissues for common resources to support their massive growth, thereby launching a vicious cycle in the neighboring tissue that gets further starved and reduced.
evidence: This is an inference based on the non-autonomous effects observed.

claim: Expressing Dilp-2 under ey-Gal4 control did not affect control eyes.
source: Whereas expressing Dilp-2 under ey-Gal4 control did not affect control eyes, it suppressed the overgrowth caused by the loss of PTEN under starvation conditions.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Expressing Dilp-2 suppressed the overgrowth caused by the loss of PTEN under starvation conditions.
source: Whereas expressing Dilp-2 under ey-Gal4 control did not affect control eyes, it suppressed the overgrowth caused by the loss of PTEN under starvation conditions.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Expressing Dilp-2 restored the growth of both the tissue surrounding the PTEN clones and peripheral tissue.
source: Furthermore, it restored the growth of both the tissue surrounding the PTEN clones and peripheral tissue (Figure 7A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The introduction of Tsc1 clones into the neighborhood of PTEN clones reduced their overgrowth under starvation.
source: Interestingly, the mutant clones did not have additive effects on overgrowth. The introduction of Tsc1 clones into the neighborhood of PTEN clones rather reduced their overgrowth under starvation.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: When neighboring with a tissue that also has a growth advantage, PTEN clones themselves experience competition for common resources.
source: Thus, when neighboring with a tissue that also has a growth advantage, PTEN clones themselves experience competition for common resources.
evidence: This is an inference based on the Tsc1 clone experiment shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Eyes with PTEN clones neighboring with TOR mutant sister clones were completely composed of PTEN mutant tissue already under standard conditions.
source: The resulting eyes were completely composed of PTEN mutant tissue already under standard conditions.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: Eyes with PTEN clones neighboring with TOR mutant sister clones were smaller as compared to eyes bearing PTEN clones only.
source: However, the eyes were smaller as compared to eyes bearing PTEN clones only.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: Clones of TOR mutant cells generated in otherwise wild-type eyes were massively underrepresented.
source: We also observed that clones of TOR mutant cells generated in otherwise wild-type eyes were massively underrepresented.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Adult eyes with TOR mutant clones were almost completely composed of wild-type twin clone tissue.
source: The adult eyes were almost completely composed of wild-type twin clone tissue (Figure 7B)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Not only PTEN mutant cells with a high growth potential but also wild-type cells neighboring with cells impaired in TORC1 function attain a growth advantage and proliferate in place of the slower growing cells.
source: The adult eyes were almost completely composed of wild-type twin clone tissue (Figure 7B), suggesting that not only PTEN mutant cells with a high growth potential but also wild-type cells neighboring with cells impaired in TORC1 function attain a growth advantage and proliferate in place of the slower growing cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the TOR mutant clone data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Relative differences in IIS activity cause a differential growth behavior.
source: Thus, relative differences in IIS activity cause a differential growth behavior.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observations with TOR and PKB mutant clones.

claim: When in competition with TOR mutant cells, PTEN clones did overgrow under NR as opposed to normal conditions.
source: Interestingly, when in competition with TOR mutant cells, PTEN clones did overgrow under NR as opposed to normal conditions (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: The overgrowth of PTEN clones when neighboring with TOR mutant cells was even more pronounced than without TOR mutant neighbors.
source: The overgrowth was even more pronounced than without TOR mutant neighbors, and it was apparent already early during larval development (Figure 7—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3.

claim: The additional overgrowth of PTEN clones when neighboring with TOR mutant cells was primarily caused by more cells.
source: SEM analysis revealed that the additional overgrowth was primarily caused by more cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 5).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 5.

claim: Ubiquitous expression of Imp-L2 caused PTEN clones to overgrow under normal conditions.
source: In this context, PTEN clones did overgrow, irrespective of whether they were neighboring with TOR mutant cells or wild-type cells (Figure 7B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The overgrowth of PTEN clones with ubiquitous Imp-L2 expression caused a further reduction in body size.
source: The overgrowth of the PTEN clones caused a further reduction in body size, as evidenced by decreased shoulder width (Figure 7B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Cells devoid of PTEN reacted to the decrease in IIS activity by slightly reducing cell size but the massive increase in cell number caused the total overgrowth.
source: Cells devoid of PTEN also reacted to the decrease in IIS activity (by slightly reducing cell size) but the massive increase in cell number caused the total overgrowth (Figure 7—figure supplement 6).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 6.

claim: Systemically decreasing IIS enhances the proliferative potential of PTEN mutant cells.
source: Thus, systemically decreasing IIS enhances the proliferative potential of PTEN mutant cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the Imp-L2 expression experiments.

claim: The loss of the tumor suppressor PTEN contributes to early clonal expansion.
source: Here, we describe how the loss of the tumor suppressor PTEN contributes to early clonal expansion.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the study's findings.

claim: PTEN mutant cells tolerate and survive starvation in a clonal situation in Drosophila imaginal discs.
source: PTEN mutant cells tolerate and survive starvation in a clonal situation in Drosophila imaginal discs.
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: The starvation tolerance response of PTEN mutant cells is completely dependent on high PKB and sustained TORC1 activities within the PTEN clones.
source: This response is completely dependent on high PKB and sustained TORC1 activities within the PTEN clones.
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the genetic interaction experiments shown in Figures 4 and 7.

claim: PTEN mutant cells acquire a growth advantage under starvation conditions at the expense of wild-type cells in the immediate neighborhood and in the entire organism.
source: PTEN mutant cells also acquire a growth advantage under starvation conditions at the expense of wild-type cells in the immediate neighborhood and in the entire organism.
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the non-autonomous effects shown in Figure 6.

claim: Activation of PI3K results in starvation insensitivity in endoreplicative tissues (ERTs).
source: It has previously been demonstrated that activation of PI3K (or of TORC1) results in starvation insensitivity in endoreplicative tissues (ERTs) (Britton et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Britton et al., 2002.

claim: ALK-dependent activation of PI3K is necessary for bypassing the amino acid requirement in growing neuroblasts under NR conditions (brain sparing).
source: Anaplastic Lymphoma Kinase (ALK)-dependent activation of PI3K is necessary for bypassing the amino acid requirement in growing neuroblasts (neural progenitors) under NR conditions (brain sparing) (Cheng et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Cheng et al., 2011.

claim: Imaginal tissues are not spared upon starvation.
source: However, imaginal tissues are not spared upon starvation, arguing against an important function of ALK in mediating growth of imaginal discs under NR conditions.
evidence: This is established knowledge about imaginal disc behavior under starvation.

claim: Mitotically active imaginal disc cells with high PIP3 levels respond differently to starvation as compared to corresponding cells in the ERTs.
source: Mitotically active imaginal disc cells with high PIP3 levels respond differently to starvation as compared to corresponding cells in the ERTs.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparing the behavior of PTEN mutant cells in imaginal discs versus ERTs.

claim: PTEN mutant imaginal disc cells do react to starvation by reducing their size like control cells do.
source: PTEN mutant imaginal disc cells do react to starvation by reducing their size like control cells do.
evidence: This is supported by the ommatidia size data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The cell size reduction in PTEN mutant cells is proportional: PTEN mutant cells are still enlarged with respect to control cells under starvation.
source: The cell size reduction is proportional: PTEN mutant cells are still enlarged with respect to control cells under starvation.
evidence: This is supported by the ommatidia size data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The cell size reduction in PTEN mutant cells is compensated for by a massive increase in proliferation, causing a net increase in mutant tissue.
source: However, the cell size reduction is compensated for by a massive increase in proliferation, causing a net increase in mutant tissue.
evidence: This is supported by the ommatidia number data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The PTEN mutant tissue is absolutely enlarged under starvation conditions.
source: In fact, the PTEN mutant tissue is absolutely enlarged under starvation conditions.
evidence: This is supported by the eye size data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: PTEN mutant cells switch from hypertrophic to hyperplastic growth under starvation.
source: PTEN mutant cells switch from hypertrophic to hyperplastic growth under starvation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the shift from increased cell size to increased cell number under starvation.

claim: The tolerance towards increased proliferation in PTEN mutant cells could favor the selection for secondary mutations that enhance proliferation and thus tumor progression.
source: This tolerance towards increased proliferation could favor the selection for secondary mutations that enhance proliferation and thus tumor progression.
evidence: This is speculation about the implications of the findings.

claim: PTEN clones display increased levels of apoptosis.
source: To our surprise, PTEN clones display increased levels of apoptosis, and selective inhibition of apoptosis within the clones results in tremendous hyperplastic overgrowth.
evidence: This is supported by the apoptosis data shown in Figure 3A-B.

claim: Selective inhibition of apoptosis within PTEN clones results in tremendous hyperplastic overgrowth.
source: To our surprise, PTEN clones display increased levels of apoptosis, and selective inhibition of apoptosis within the clones results in tremendous hyperplastic overgrowth.
evidence: This is supported by the p35 expression data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The induction of apoptosis in PTEN mutant tissue contrasts the known pro-survival function of PKB.
source: The induction of apoptosis in PTEN mutant tissue contrasts the known pro-survival function of PKB (Scanga et al., 2000).
evidence: This is an observation that contrasts with established knowledge, supported by citation.

claim: The starved PTEN mutant cells, despite their proliferative advantage, exist on the edge of survival and are highly susceptible to apoptosis.
source: However, it indicates that the starved PTEN mutant cells, despite their proliferative advantage, exist on the edge of survival and are highly susceptible to apoptosis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the high apoptosis levels in PTEN clones.

claim: Acquisition of factors preventing apoptosis would strongly enhance the growth of tumors lacking PTEN.
source: Our findings also suggest that acquisition of factors preventing apoptosis would strongly enhance the growth of tumors lacking PTEN.
evidence: This is speculation based on the p35 expression results.

claim: PTEN clones impact on IIS activity in the surrounding tissue, thereby reducing its growth potential.
source: Furthermore, cells neighboring with PTEN mutant tissue are smaller than those in the discs containing control clones. Thus, PTEN clones impact on IIS activity in the surrounding tissue, thereby reducing its growth potential.
evidence: This is an inference based on the P-PKB levels and cell size in surrounding tissue shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The non-autonomous growth reduction by PTEN clones is sufficient to explain the strong reduction of the surrounding tissue.
source: This appears to be sufficient to explain the strong reduction of the surrounding tissue, since the process of ousting the neighboring tissue is completed as early as 60 hr after clonal induction, when the disc still contains relatively few cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the time-course data.

claim: The non-autonomous growth reduction by PTEN clones is not restricted to the local neighbors in a cell–cell contact-dependent manner, but rather affects all tissues of the organism.
source: This non-autonomous growth reduction is not restricted to the local neighbors in a cell–cell contact-dependent manner, but rather affects all tissues of the organism.
evidence: This is supported by the systemic effects shown in Figure 6B-D.

claim: The cells compete for common factors, most likely growth factors and nutrients.
source: The impact of PTEN mutant tissue on its surroundings suggests that the cells compete for common factors, most likely growth factors and nutrients.
evidence: This is an inference based on the non-autonomous effects and the rescue by Dilp-2 expression.

claim: Under starvation, the circulating levels of growth factors and nutrients are strongly reduced, and thereby can become limiting.
source: Under starvation, the circulating levels of growth factors and nutrients are strongly reduced, and thereby can become limiting (Cheng et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Drosophila insulin-like peptides (DILPs) produced by the insulin-producing cells (IPCs) in the brain stimulate the growth of imaginal disc cells via the InR.
source: Drosophila insulin-like peptides (DILPs) produced by the insulin-producing cells (IPCs) in the brain stimulate the growth of imaginal disc cells via the InR.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Drosophila insulin signaling.

claim: Starvation reduces the secretion of DILPs from the IPCs, and thus reduces growth.
source: Starvation reduces the secretion of DILPs from the IPCs, and thus reduces growth (Geminard et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Despite lacking the signal input via InR, PTEN mutant cells are able to accumulate PIP3, probably because of the basal activity of PI3K.
source: Thus, despite lacking the signal input via InR, these cells are able to accumulate PIP3, probably because of the basal activity of PI3K.
evidence: This is an inference based on the InR removal experiment.

claim: Low levels of circulating DILPs are sufficient to boost PIP3 levels and PKB activity in PTEN mutant cells under starvation.
source: Therefore, low levels of circulating DILPs are sufficient to boost PIP3 levels and PKB activity in PTEN mutant cells under starvation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the high PIP3 and P-PKB levels in PTEN clones under starvation.

claim: In contrast to inhibiting TORC1 activity, reducing Slif does not block the initial overgrowth of PTEN clones under starvation.
source: We show that, in contrast to inhibiting TORC1 activity, reducing Slif does not block the initial overgrowth of PTEN clones under starvation.
evidence: This is supported by the time-course data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Reducing Slif causes the overgrown PTEN clones to collapse.
source: However, it causes the overgrown clones to collapse.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 5A-B.

claim: The high metabolic demands of PTEN mutant cells require an efficient amino acid uptake, which is blocked by reducing Slif.
source: We speculate that the high metabolic demands of PTEN mutant cells require an efficient amino acid uptake, which is blocked by reducing Slif.
evidence: This is speculation based on the Slif knockdown results.

claim: PTEN mutant cells rely on their ability to efficiently compete for nutrients and growth factors under starvation conditions with their direct neighbors and the peripheral tissue.
source: Thus, PTEN mutant cells rely on their ability to efficiently compete for nutrients and growth factors under starvation conditions with their direct neighbors and the peripheral tissue.
evidence: This is an inference based on the overall findings of the study.

claim: The reduction of Slif affects the growth of the wild-type and the PTEN mutant tissue in a differential manner.
source: Since the reduction of Slif affects the growth of the wild-type and the PTEN mutant tissue in a differential manner, this amino acid transporter could represent a target for a dosage-dependent drug therapy of tumors with PI3K activation.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Slimfast could represent a target for a dosage-dependent drug therapy of tumors with PI3K activation.
source: Since the reduction of Slif affects the growth of the wild-type and the PTEN mutant tissue in a differential manner, this amino acid transporter could represent a target for a dosage-dependent drug therapy of tumors with PI3K activation.
evidence: This is speculation about potential therapeutic applications.

claim: Under starvation conditions, circulating growth factors and nutrients are scarce.
source: Under starvation conditions, circulating growth factors and nutrients are scarce.
evidence: This is established knowledge about starvation responses.

claim: Both wild-type and PTEN mutant cells adjust their growth with respect to cellular size in response to limited resources.
source: In response to these limited resources, both wild-type and PTEN mutant cells adjust their growth with respect to cellular size.
evidence: This is supported by the ommatidia size data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: In sharp contrast to wild-type clones, PTEN clones retain high PI3K activity and strongly increase their cell number.
source: In sharp contrast to wild-type clones, PTEN clones retain high PI3K activity and strongly increase their cell number.
evidence: This is supported by the PIP3 levels (Figure 4A) and ommatidia number data (Figure 2E).

claim: The hyperplastic clonal overgrowth of PTEN clones depends on withdrawing nutrients from the neighborhood and ultimately the entire organism.
source: This hyperplastic clonal overgrowth depends on withdrawing nutrients from the neighborhood and ultimately the entire organism.
evidence: This is an inference based on the non-autonomous effects shown in Figure 6.

claim: The active scavenging of resources by PTEN clones is dependent on efficient amino acid transporters (Slif).
source: The active scavenging of resources is dependent on efficient amino acid transporters (Slif), which also ensure that TORC1 remains active.
evidence: This is supported by the Slif knockdown experiments shown in Figure 5.

claim: Efficient amino acid transporters ensure that TORC1 remains active in PTEN clones.
source: The active scavenging of resources is dependent on efficient amino acid transporters (Slif), which also ensure that TORC1 remains active.
evidence: This is an inference based on the role of Slif in TORC1 activation.

claim: During their entire growth, PTEN mutant cells are at the brink of death as evidenced by the high apoptosis rate within the PTEN clones.
source: During their entire growth, cells are at the brink of death as evidenced by the high apoptosis rate within the PTEN clones.
evidence: This is supported by the apoptosis data shown in Figure 3A-B.

claim: Enhanced PIP3 levels in cells that lost the tumor suppressor PTEN leads to starvation resistance at the cellular level.
source: Thus, enhanced PIP3 levels in cells that lost the tumor suppressor PTEN not only leads to starvation resistance at the cellular level, but also suppresses growth in their direct tissue neighborhood and in peripheral tissues by competing for nutrients and growth factors.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the study's findings.

claim: Enhanced PIP3 levels in PTEN mutant cells suppress growth in their direct tissue neighborhood and in peripheral tissues by competing for nutrients and growth factors.
source: Thus, enhanced PIP3 levels in cells that lost the tumor suppressor PTEN not only leads to starvation resistance at the cellular level, but also suppresses growth in their direct tissue neighborhood and in peripheral tissues by competing for nutrients and growth factors.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the study's findings.

claim: Limiting nutrient conditions enhance the proliferative potential of PTEN mutant cells, independent of additional genetic alterations.
source: Our findings demonstrate how limiting nutrient conditions enhance the proliferative potential of PTEN mutant cells, independent of additional genetic alterations.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the study's findings.
